corpus.title: UAE Calls Flydubai Attack ‘Terrorist Act’ for First Time as Israel Probes if Hijacker ‘Was Sent’
corpus.signal_text:
A senior United Arab Emirates official on Friday publicly described the attempted crashing of a Flydubai passenger jet as a “terrorist act” for the first time, as Israel investigates if the Omani co-pilot accused of trying to bring down the aircraft was acting on behalf of another party.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that the co-pilot had previously been banned by Oman from flying, over concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views, citing people familiar with the matter. Despite the ban, the Omani national was later hired by Flydubai and allowed to fly the sensitive route connecting the United Arab Emirates and Israel.
It remains unclear if Oman shared its concerns about the co-pilot with other countries or airlines, and the nature of his reported radicalization could not be determined, according to the report. Flydubai and the Omani government did not respond to requests for comment.
A UAE spokesperson declined to address the co-pilot’s reported history in Oman, saying that doing so could “prejudge the outcome of the investigation or interfere with its course.”
The report emerged as Anwar Gargash, a senior diplomatic adviser to UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed, publicly characterized Wednesday’s attack as terrorism while praising Capt. Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who was repeatedly stabbed aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
“The Flydubai pilot deserves full appreciation,” Gargash wrote on X. “Faced with a dangerous terrorist act and a possible disaster, he embodied the true meaning of courage and responsibility.”
“The professionalism and moral integrity he demonstrated under the most challenging circumstances make him a true hero,” he added.
Gargash’s remarks marked the first time a senior Emirati official publicly characterized the incident as terrorism, sharpening the UAE’s public position a day after authorities opened an investigation into whether the attack was linked to terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction.
Gargash nevertheless cautioned against drawing conclusions beyond what investigators have established.
“While avoiding interpretations or promoting conspiracy theories, vigilance and caution remain essential in confronting the dangers of extremism and terrorism,” he wrote.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, said Friday that Israel is investigating whether the Omani co-pilot “was sent,” while stopping short of identifying who, if anyone, may have directed him.

Captain Smit Machchhar spoke to Indian PM in interview broadcast live from hospital
The Indian airline captain who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a FlyDubai flight described Friday how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent.
Captain Smit Machchhar, recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call broadcast live on television news channels that he knew he had to get back on his feet to save the passengers aboard the aircraft.
"I had so many wounds. I had fallen down," he said from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack.
"I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realized that if I didn't get up … then passengers would lose their lives," he told Modi.

"Lord Hanuman gave me courage," he told Modi.

Initial findings from the UAE’s investigation into the attack also did not confirm his nationality, according to a report today from the country’s state news agency WAM, but a Saudi source has confirmed to AFP that he was Omani.
Media reports have also said he had been barred from flying in his home nation over concerns about extremist views.
The reports came as the first flight carrying Israelis home from the United Arab Emirates landed in Tel Aviv after services were suspended following the attack, according to Israel’s airport authority website.
“The co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist act” and had “attacked the captain in the cockpit with the emergency axe and tried to take control of the aircraft”, WAM quoted UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying, referring to initial findings of an investigation.
The co-pilot is still in custody in the UAE. Multiple media outlets overnight identified him as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami and said he had been banned from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.
During the flydubai flight, the plane’s Indian captain was assaulted by the co-pilot but the captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Passengers described rushing the cockpit and a fight for control after the plane plummeted — losing around 17,000 feet of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website.

Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, has been named as the suspect and co-pilot of the Boeing 747 Flydubai jet, which had 182 people on board, most of them Israeli nationals.
Passengers and crew stormed the cockpit to overpower the attacker and seize control of the plane during the apparent attempt to down a flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday.
The plane plummeted about 16,625ft in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the UAE to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24.

‘Axe used in attempted terror attack’
The suspect is now being held in the UAE, where the prosecutor-general said on Saturday that the co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe and tried to seize control of the plane.
A crash axe is usually kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies.
“Investigations into the incident involving Flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack,” Emirates News Agency WAM quoted UAE prosecutor-general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi as saying.
The UAE official’s comments were the first by Emirati authorities to describe the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.
Lone wolf?
A Gulf diplomat said investigations are under way to establish whether the suspect acted as a “lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups”.
The circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections are being probed, including through examination of physical and digital evidence, the prosecutor-general has said.
The UAE is leading the investigation as the airline is owned by Dubai’s government.

Hammami, the suspected attacker, was barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a person familiar with the matter told Associated Press.
The co-pilot was subsequently hired by the Dubai airline, the person said.
